text: An Online Stability Indicator for Real-Time Hybrid Simulation Emphasizing Physical Substructure Degradation
Mohamed Gomaa,2,  Edwin D. Patino, Juan Nicolas Villamizar2, Johnny W. Condori Uribe, Shirley J. Dyke
Abstract

Real-time hybrid simulation (RTHS) has become increasingly important as an experimental tool for evaluating system-level structural response under realistic loading while averting the cost and impracticality of full-scale testing. Recent advances in real-time processing, high-quality sensing, and servo-hydraulic control techniques have accelerated RTHS adoption and enabled more complex experiments. However, a key barrier to reliable RTHS execution remains the potential loss of stability as the physical substructure evolves during testing, particularly under stiffness degradation. This paper addresses this challenge by first formulating a typical RTHS framework and transfer-system dynamics, then analyzing stability under a parameterized degradation of the physical substructure and presenting a computational procedure for determining the critical damage level. Building on this analysis, an online stability indicator based on the normalized coprime factor (NCF) margin is presented and simplified for efficient evaluation in single-input-single-output (SISO) settings. A controller-switching strategy is also demonstrated to support practical intervention during an experiment by transitioning from a high-performance controller to a high-robustness controller as stability margins diminish. The switching boundary is formulated using Lyapunov stability criteria to ensure closed-loop stability during the transition. The approach is demonstrated on a modified version of a well-established benchmark problem. Using virtual real-time hybrid simulation (vRTHS), the proposed indicator is shown to provide a timely warning of diminishing robustness, enabling a smooth controller transition that successfully maintains stable operation and response accuracy under progressive degradation.
Keywords: real-time hybrid simulation; stability indicator; normalized coprime factor; structural degradation; controller switching
1-Introduction

Despite the remarkable advances in computational modeling and simulation tools, experimental testing remains indispensable to provide sufficient understanding of complex structural systems. Computational models often rely on idealized assumptions and simplifications, and their applicability may be limited when dealing with new, untested innovations. Experimental calibration and validation may be required before they are likely to be adopted for predicting the response to new inputs [1].

The ideal experiment to provide the most realistic test conditions and accurate results would be a full-scale, real-time experiment. However, such a test is often infeasible due to the cost, time, scale, and physical constraints, especially for structural applications. These constraints inspired civil engineering researchers to embark on a multi-decade effort to establish cost-effective testing methods that provide meaningful data for understanding behavior, validating models, and capturing the full spectrum of responses up to failure. One testing method that has been a fundamental part of civil engineering research since the early 20th century is the quasi-static technique [2]. With this approach, a predefined loading input is applied to a structural component (e.g., a building column or bridge pier) at a slow rate to allow close observation of the evolution of damage and to determine the hysteretic behavior without the need for high-performance actuators. As a result of its nature, the quasi-static technique has some major limitations: 1) it focuses on obtaining component-level rather than structure-level information, and thus it neglects the interaction between the component being tested and the rest of the structure; 2) it requires a predefined loading protocol, which helps in understanding some of the mechanical component properties, but it may not reflect the actual, or the full range, of structural behavior during the real situation; and, 3) its inherently slow loading rate prevents it from capturing rate-dependent phenomena [3].

These shortcomings motivated a new, cost-effective and efficient experimental technique to evaluate the dynamic performance of large civil structures. Hybrid simulation (HS) has emerged to fill this role, finding its way into structural engineering in the late 1960s [4]. In HS, the structure under investigation is partitioned into two parts: a physical substructure and a numerical substructure. Typically, the physical substructure includes the more complex components of the system, while the numerical substructure models the portions that are well-understood. The interaction between the two substructures is maintained by a transfer system, comprising servo-hydraulic actuators, sensors, and controllers, that enforce compatibility conditions at their interface [5].

As a natural evolution of HS, real-time hybrid simulation (RTHS) was developed to capture rate-dependent properties of systems. Despite being a powerful and versatile testing methodology, RTHS posed new challenges to the research community, as the accuracy of the results is strongly influenced by the performance of the transfer system. Good performance requires both appropriate selection of the hardware and careful design of the controllers, which typically need to be customized to meet the test objectives and account for the unique dynamics of each experiment [6], [7]. Inadequate controller design may not only compromise the accuracy of the results, but also induce instability in the system, potentially creating safety hazards or damaging costly equipment.

To address these challenges, significant research has been carried out to establish the knowledge to improve a transfer system’s performance and stability. For instance, Dyke et al. [8] presented a substantial insight into understanding the physical substructure dynamics as they explained control-structure interaction and showed that actuators have an implicit feedback interaction path. Further, Carrion [6] and Maghareh et al. [9] studied transfer system modelling and developed a parametric model that describes the physical substructure dynamics, thereby laying the foundation for subsequent analytical investigations. Recognizing the need for collaborative progress and to provide a shared testbed that helps researchers standardize the evaluation process of diverse algorithms, benchmark problems were proposed for single-degree-of-freedom [10] and multi-degree-of-freedom [11] controlled substructures. These benchmarks have engaged a wide research community and led to notable advances in the field, with several studies demonstrating successful and effective implementations [12], [13], [14], [15], [16]. Additionally, more studies extended the framework to incorporate nonlinear experimental components, confirming the versatility of RTHS in capturing complex behaviors [17].

The promising use of RTHS has motivated extensive stability studies to empower researchers to execute more complex experiments. Foundational work to study the RTHS stability analytically was established by Gawthrop et al. [18] and Mercan & Ricles [19], who used delay differential equations to determine system delay margins. These initial works, however, were limited by the simplifying assumption that the experimental substructure had stiffness and damping only. This limitation was addressed by Chi et al. [20], Wallace et al. [21], and Kyrychko et al. [22], who extended the study to include single degree of freedom (SDOF) physical substructures with both stiffness and mass properties. Additionally, they studied the instability mechanism that arises based on the physical substructure properties. To broaden the scope of the investigation, Gao & You [23] and Zhu et al. [24] extended the delay-based indicators to multi-degree-of-freedom (MDOF) systems in their stability studies. Maghareh et al. [5] leveraged the critical delay and derived an efficient eigenvalue-based solution providing a means for selecting among multiple partitioning schemes. To address the need for real-time monitoring, Gálmez & Fermandois [25] and Ahmadizadeh & Mosqueda [26] studied an efficient, energy-based stability indicator for online monitoring. By relying on observed signals during the experiment, it avoids dependence on an explicit model of the transfer system and can be implemented with minimal overhead. However, since it is not predictive and relies on observed data, it cannot provide a tunable lead-time margin for safety interventions. It is therefore well-suited as a secondary safety layer alongside primary predictive indicator aware of the system dynamics.

One common assumption in the aforementioned RTHS stability studies is the reduction of the entire transfer system, including actuator dynamics and potential disruptions, to a lumped pure time delay effect. While being convenient for analysis and design, this model is an approximation and may fail to capture fundamentally different instability mechanisms, such as gain amplification driven by unmodeled dynamics or stiffness degradation.

Recognizing these limitations, Tang et al. [27] developed a gain-margin-based stability boundary predictor that explicitly accounts for high-order servo-hydraulic transfer-system dynamics with simultaneously varying magnitude and phase, showing that the common pure-delay assumption has a low-frequency validity limit and validating the new method experimentally on a shaking-table test. Moreover, H. Zhou et al. [28] proposed a relative stability indicator for RTHS that relies on two quantitative robustness measures, critical delay for phase tolerance and critical gain, and validated it by numerical and physical SDOF tests. In these studies, the physical substructure parameters are not constant over the course of the experiment, however, the stability indicators are evaluated using a pre-identified loop model and are not updated online as the dynamics evolve. Moreover, extending these methods to multi-input-multi-output (MIMO) systems is non-trivial, particularly for coupled MDOF systems where complex actuator interactions complicate the analysis. Table 1 provides a comparative summary of the RTHS stability indicators in literature, highlighting their capabilities across the selected evaluation criteria.

As shown in Table 1, most prior work adopts a lumped pure time-delay representation of the transfer system, which is referred to in this study as a low-fidelity representation. While this simplification enables stability assessment of the numerical substructure loop (shown in purple in Figure 1, it does not capture the dynamics of the outer controller loop (shown in blue in Figure 2, and therefore cannot evaluate its stability. Depending on the system dynamics and the disruption type, the outer controller loop can be the governing stability constraint. In this study, we present an example where physical-substructure degradation destabilizes the system while monitoring the global loop of the numerical substructure indicates enhanced robustness, motivating the importance of investigating the stability of the outer controller loop by employing high-fidelity models for the transfer system.

Although gain and delay margins are informative for offline experiment design and partitioning selection, computing them online for high-fidelity transfer system models is inherently challenging due to the computational burden of tracking multiple crossover frequencies and maintaining numerical stability in real time. Furthermore, extending these indicators to MIMO configurations introduces additional complications, as the standard loop-at-a-time extension, which perturbs one input/output channel while holding the others nominal, can be overly optimistic, as it ignores coupled, simultaneous variations across channels [32]. On the other hand, energy-based indicators are largely observation-driven, as they are computed from measured response histories and error accumulation rather than explicit model-based predictions. Consequently, they provide limited ability to define a tunable lead time for proactive intervention.

To address these gaps, we propose an online stability indicator with a focus on the internal stability of the transfer system and its robustness against unmodeled disruptions. In establishing the indicator, special attention is given to physical system degradation, considering it as the most prevalent disruption to the plant during an RTHS experiment. An analytical solution quantifying the system's robustness to such degradation is presented, and the indicator's performance is illustrated through an example that is adapted from the RTHS benchmark problem. The proposed framework further integrates this online indicator with a controller-switching strategy to enable proactive intervention as robustness decreases. The switching boundary is established using Lyapunov stability criteria to preserve closed-loop stability during the transition.

The paper is structured to sequentially develop and demonstrate the proposed framework. Section 2 establishes the RTHS problem formulation and the high-fidelity transfer-system model used throughout the study. Section 3 investigates the effect of physical-substructure degradation on outer-loop stability and derives the corresponding degradation-dependent stability boundary. Section 4 provides the technical background on classical and modern robustness measures and uses this progression to introduce and formulate the NCF-based online stability indicator. Section 5 develops the controller-switching framework and examines the stability of the transition using Lyapunov criteria. Section 6 demonstrates the complete framework through an illustrative vRTHS example involving nonlinear specimen degradation and controller switching. Finally, Section 7 summarizes the main findings and conclusions.
2-Problem Formulation

The fundamental concept of RTHS is to partition a reference structural model into two substructures. Therefore, an RTHS consists of several major components, including: (i) a numerical substructure that can be evaluated in real-time on a computer; (ii) a physical substructure excited by actuators and instrumented with sensors; and, (iii) a transfer system, comprising the controller, servo-valve and actuator hydraulics, that enforces compatibility and equilibrium interface by synchronizing the physical substructure's response with the numerical evaluated response. Figure 1 illustrates a typical RTHS scheme where the numerical substructure is subjected to a ground acceleration, agt, where dd is the calculated desired displacement from the numerical model, and fe is the measured force from the physical substructure, while Figure 2 provides a closer look inside the transfer system block. Although seismic excitation is used for illustration in this study, the proposed framework is not restricted to earthquake loading and can be applied to other external excitations, such as wind loading, by modifying the corresponding input to the numerical substructure.

Mrxt+Crxt+Krxt=-MrΓagt# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 1

where Mr, Cr, and Kr are the mass, damping, and stiffness matrices, xt, xt and xt are the displacement, velocity, and acceleration vectors, agt is the ground acceleration, Γ is the influence vector mapping base motion to the active DOFs.
Then the partitioning is performed:
Mr=Mn+Me, Cr=Cn+Ce, Kr=Kn+Ke# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 2
where the subscripts n and e denote the numerical and experimental substructures contributions, respectively. By substituting these into Equation (1) and rearranging:
Mnx+Cnx+Knx=-MrΓag-Mex+Cex+Kex# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 3
Mnxn+Cnxn+Knxn=-MrΓag+fe# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 4

Equation (4) represents the cornerstone to model the numerical substructure block which actively computes the required responses to be imposed on the physical substructure. Realizing this response is where the transfer system is engaged to ensure precise tracking and maintain stability in this process.

The transfer-system formulation adopted here follows Maghareh et al. [29], where actuator-force feedback, oil column stiffness, and control-structure interaction are included in the transfer-system formulation through the lumped parameters a1,a2,and a3.
As shown in Figure 2, the transfer system can be represented by five blocks that represent its dynamic behavior, as follows:

i) Servo-valve: connects the electrical and mechanical parts of the system as it regulates the flow of high-pressure hydraulic oil into the actuator chambers. Despite the fact that its behavior often involves nonlinearities and higher-order dynamics, it can often be simplified to first-order or second-order dynamics [6], [29], [30]. Thus, the servo-valve block Ga1 can be modeled in the frequency domain as:
Ga1s=a1β0s2+β1s+β2.# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 5

ii) Hydraulic actuator: converts the hydraulic energy into mechanical energy as a force or displacement that is imposed to the physical specimen. Assuming a double-ended linear actuator is used, its behavior can be represented using a first-order transfer function [6]. Thus, the actuator block Ga3 can be modeled as follows:
Ga3s=1s+a3# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 6

iii) Control-structure interaction (CSI): represents the inherent physical coupling between the actuator and the experimental structure. As shown in [8], it can be represented by the following expression:
Ga2s=a2s# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 7
iv) Inner loop controller: typically, a hardware-based proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller provided with the servo-hydraulic system.

v) Outer loop controller: a user-defined controller where sophisticated control and compensation algorithms may be implemented. It should be executed on a real-time computer, taking in the target displacement from the numerical substructure and generating the command signal to send to the inner loop controller.

Finally, the physical substructure block represents the structural components that are being tested. For a single-degree-of-freedom (SDOF) linear structural system, the following expression can be used:
Gss=1ms2+cs+k# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 8
where m, c, and k  are the mass, damping coefficient, and stiffness of the specimen, respectively.
Moreover, the transfer function of a degraded physical substructure can be defined as:
Gss,α=1ms2+2ζmαks+αk# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 9

where  α is a degradation factor ranging from 1 for a healthy structure to 0 for a completely damaged structure, and ζ is the damping ratio. Note that the degradation factor relates specifically to the loss in stiffness. This simplified stiffness-degradation model is needed to obtain a theoretical formulation of the stability boundary. In practice, degradation may also change other properties, particularly damping. However, increased damping has been shown to improve RTHS stability [31]. Therefore, neglecting any additional damping introduced by degradation represents a conservative assumption with respect to this effect.

To address the nonlinear and time-varying nature of structural degradation, a short-window linear approximation is used to keep the analysis tractable and suitable for online evaluation. Although this method may not be accurate during brief intervals where properties change rapidly, it is typically accurate before and after such events, and during periods where degradation evolves slowly.

With the real-time hybrid simulation (RTHS) framework blocks defined, a vRTHS is performed to evaluate various stability indicators. This analysis considers a three-story reference building where a portion of the first story acts as the physical substructure represented by an SDOF frame. More details on this study are provided in section 6. The stability analysis begins by simulating a healthy structure (α=1) and then progressively reducing the degradation factor, α​, to simulate the accumulation of damage. The level of specimen degradation is increased in this way to allow the system to approach an instability and illustrate the target behavior.

To motivate the need for an alternative stability metric and to establish a baseline for comparison, three potential stability indicators (SIs) are evaluated, including: (i) numerical critical time delay (τcr,N), defined as the maximum time delay that can be added to the numerical substructure's feedback loop before the system becomes unstable. Its evaluation typically relies on a simplified model where the entire transfer system is represented as a lumped pure time delay, as depicted in Figure 3 [5]. (ii) physical critical time delay (τcr,P), defined as the maximum time delay that can be added to the outer loop controller's feedback loop (indicated in blue in Figure 2) before instability occurs, and (iii) the physical controller gain margin (GMP), which represents the maximum constant gain that can be applied to the outer loop controller's feedback loop. The outcome of these indicators during progressive structural damage is illustrated in Figure 4. The horizontal axis represents the degradation factor, α , while the vertical axis shows each SI's value, normalized by its initial value for the healthy structure. Normalization is used to focus the analysis on the qualitative behavior and sensitivity of each indicator to degradation, rather than their absolute magnitudes.

Interpreting Figure 4 reveals that both critical time delay indicators ( τcr,N and τcr,P) fail to accurately reflect the growing risk of instability arising from structural damage. Specifically, τcr,N exhibits misleading behavior as its normalized value increases with damage, falsely suggesting enhanced stability, while τcr,P remained nearly constant until exhibiting an abrupt drop, offering no advance warning. In contrast, the  GMP exhibits a more gradual decrease before the onset of instability, suggesting that the instability triggered by the degradation is closer to being caused by a gain amplification in the outer controller loop than a time delay, a mechanism that delay margins struggle to detect. To further illustrate this behavior, Figure 5 shows the corresponding open-loop gain and phase responses of Hymy1, highlighting how the outer-loop dynamics evolve with physical substructure degradation and can lead to instabilities.

Based on our observations in the laboratory, this instability is caused by the controller being initially tuned to both overcome the specimen's relatively high stiffness and also achieve the required tracking performance. As the specimen degrades and loses stiffness, it becomes easier to move, so the same corrective control action is likely to overshoot more and produce a larger displacement response than under the original stiffness condition. The extent of this response amplification is influenced by the specimen mass, and the resulting interaction between the degraded specimen and the transfer system, which includes this controller, can eventually drive the system toward instability. It's important to note that, despite being observed experimentally, these behaviors are not universal, as the dominant instability mechanism and the performance of each indicator can change substantially depending on the specific dynamics of the transfer system and the physical substructure.

This study aims to present an online stability indicator for quantifying the system's robustness against different instability mechanisms driven by unmodeled dynamics or unforeseen disruptions, while also aiming to provide a sufficient time frame for effective intervention before instability occurs. To address a notable gap in the literature, this study focuses on the transfer system's internal stability, giving special consideration to physical system degradation, as it can manifest during an experiment in various forms, including, but not limited to, excessive specimen damage, the activation of unintended structural failure mechanisms, or the mechanical failure of test set-up components such as fasteners. Additionally, a controller switching strategy is proposed to leverage the stability indicator for real-time corrective action when degradation threatens system stability.

3-Stability Analysis of RTHS Under Structural Degradation

Physical substructure degradation constitutes a prevalent and often unavoidable phenomenon in realistic RTHS experiments. Such degradation can arise in various forms including gradual processes (e.g., steel bar yielding or fastener loosening) or more abrupt processes (e.g., concrete fracture or fastener rupture). As previously demonstrated in Figure 4, this degradation in physical substructure can drive the system toward instability through mechanisms that are not adequately captured by traditional time delay metrics. In this section, a closed-form solution for the instability boundary is provided as a function of the structural degradation ratio. Subsequently, this framework is leveraged to investigate the relationship between the physical substructure's initial dynamics and its capacity to tolerate damage before the onset of instability. The following derivation assumes the specimen dynamics can be approximated as linear within short windows of time using an equivalent stiffness, noting that real damage can alter more than a reduction in stiffness and those additional effects are not modeled explicitly but are treated as unmodeled dynamics. Alongside this assumption, the specimen mass is assumed to be constant over the test duration.

To derive the stability boundary, the system is simplified by reducing the block diagram of the transfer system demonstrated in Figure 2. By focusing on an SDOF physical substructure subjected to damage, the definition of Gss,α given in Equation 9 can be utilized. Starting from the innermost loop and moving outwards, for completeness, intermediate transfer functions are defined.

which expands to:
Hym y5s,α=Gss,αGa3s1+Gss,αGa3sGa2s# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 12

The transfer system operates under a unity gain feedback scheme with an open-loop transfer function of Ls,α=CoutsTs,α. System stability is therefore determined by the roots of the characteristic equation:
1+Ls,α=0# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 17

This equation defines the poles of the closed-loop system. According to classical control theory, the system is stable if and only if all roots of this equation lie strictly in the left half of the complex plane. Instability arises if any root has a positive real part, indicating the presence of an unstable mode in the structural response.
Expanding the expression for 1+Ls,α provides the system's full characteristic equation,
1+Ls,α=

To find the system's poles, the numerator is set to zero and the equation is solved. This approach implicitly ignores poles that are canceled by zeros. These specific poles correspond to the stability of the inner loops (the inner loop controller and CSI loops). Therefore, assuming these loops are already stable, the numerator is set to zero and we factor the expression, which gives:
1+Gss,αGa3sGa2s+CinsGa1sGa3s+CoutsCinsGa1sGa3s=0# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 19
For clarity, the bracketed term is defined as Ys:
Ys≔Ga3sGa2s+CinsGa1sCouts+1# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 20
This step allows the stability boundary condition to be expressed in the following simplified form:
1+Gss,αYs=0# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 21

A key strength of this formulation lies in its decoupling of the degradation-dependent physical specimen, which is a function of α, from the rest of the transfer system components, encapsulated in the composite function Ys. This analytical separation allows solving for the stability boundary in terms of the degradation factor, α, directly.
By substituting Gss,α into this equation, the stability condition can be expressed in terms of the structural parameters, as
1+Ysms2+2ζmαk s+αk=0# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 22
This step leads us to the final form of the characteristic equation, which is denoted as CEs,α:
CEs,α=ms2+2ζmαks+αk+Ys=0# SEQ Equation \* ARABIC \* MERGEFORMAT 23

Since controllers are typically designed based on a healthy system, the poles initially lie in the left-half complex plane. The experiment begins with α=1 (the undamaged state), and as damage accumulates (α decreases), the poles shift gradually towards the imaginary axis. Instability occurs when a pole reaches this axis (Res=0), providing a condition to solve for the degradation factor, α, and the corresponding oscillation frequency, ω. The critical degradation ratio, αcr ​, is thus defined as the maximum value of α  for which the equation CEjω,α has a real solution for  ω, that is

3.2-Linking Structural Properties to RTHS Robustness

To investigate the relationship between the initial properties of a physical substructure and its damage tolerance, a parametric study is conducted on a family of structural specimens. These specimens are defined by varying the mass (m) and stiffness (k) parameters, with each system’s robustness evaluated by solving for αcr leveraging Equations (31) and (29). To maintain consistent performance and stability margins, outer and inner controllers are redesigned offline to achieve a target crossover frequency and phase margin for each specimen configuration.

The relationship between the specimen parameters (mass m and initial stiffness ko) and the critical degradation ratio, shown in Figure 6, shows that increasing the specimen mass and reducing the initial stiffness-to-mass ratio, which corresponds to a more flexible structure in its original undamaged state, leads to higher critical degradation ratios. Since higher αcr values indicate greater susceptibility to instability, the findings suggest that more flexible structures are more prone to loss of control stability and thus require more careful stability analysis. To be consistent with the benchmark, a damping ratio of 1% was used to generate the figure. Two specific configurations are highlighted: one marker corresponds to the benchmark statement provided in [10], and the other to a modified configuration used in the illustrative example presented later in this study. In the modified configuration, the specimen mass is increased by 30% relative to the benchmark, making the initially healthy structure more flexible and therefore more susceptible to instability.

A lower αcr reflects a system that is more robust to physical degradation. The parameter configurations for both the original and modified benchmark problems are indicated by markers.

Since the objective is to support safe experiment execution, the damping ratio is conservatively assumed to remain constant during degradation avoiding the high uncertainties and practical difficulties of reliably estimating the specimen’s evolving damping during a test. However, to provide insight regarding how damping would affect these values, increasing the ζ from 1% to 2% and 5% would improve stability by reducing αcr from approximately 0.275 to 0.247 and 0.187, respectively.
4-Integration into an RTHS Framework

The preceding section presented a numerical method for quantifying system robustness specifically against structural degradation. This section expands upon that foundation to develop a stability indicator that can be used during an experiment. The goal is to develop a metric that not only offers a continuous, real-time assessment of the system’s actual robustness but also accounts for a wider range of uncertainties that may arise during an experiment.

The foundational principles for quantifying stability in linear time-invariant feedback systems were established in the 1930s and 1940s through the pioneering work of Harry Nyquist and Hendrik Bode [32], [33]. Their approach was revolutionary as it introduced a graphical approach based on the frequency domain, allowing for stability assessment without calculating the system’s poles. Using their now-famous Nyquist and Bode plots, they developed two enduring and fundamental metrics for measuring system robustness: the Gain Margin (GM) and the Phase Margin (PM). These margins were determined by geometrically inspecting the plots, providing a practical way to assess system robustness.

The first of these metrics, GM, is defined as the factor by which the open-loop gain can be increased before the system reaches the point of instability. This value can be interpreted from either of the graphical methods: on a Bode plot, as demonstrated in Figure 7(a), the GM is found by measuring the vertical distance between the 0 dB line and the magnitude curve at the frequency where the phase shift is equal to -180°. On a Nyquist plot, it is the reciprocal of the magnitude where the curve intersects the negative real axis as shown in Figure 7(b). While there is no universal standard, a minimum GM of 6 decibels is often considered to be sufficient for adequate robustness  [34].

The other fundamental metric is the PM, defined as the amount of additional open-loop phase lag needed to destabilize the closed-loop system at its unity-gain frequency. As illustrated in Figure 7(a), the PM on a Bode plot is the vertical distance between the phase curve and the  -180° line at this gain crossover frequency. Equivalently, on a Nyquist plot, it is the angle between the negative real axis and the point where the contour intersects the unit circle, as depicted in Figure 7(b).

Imposing a constant phase shift across the entire frequency spectrum yields a physically unrealizable system. In contrast, a time delay offers a more realistic model by introducing a phase lag that increases with frequency. This approach leads to another important metric, the Delay Margin (DM), which can be approximated from the PM using the expression DM≈PM/ωgc [35]. Since many RTHS components are more likely to introduce delays rather than amplify gains to the inner loop system, prior studies have often considered the DM as the most descriptive indicator of system robustness. To ensure robust performance and adequate system damping, a PM of 45 to 60 degrees is often considered a desirable design target [36].

One significant limitation of the GM and PM indicators is that they can create a false sense of security [37]. This limitation is primarily present because they are fundamentally uncoupled indicators, evaluating robustness to either pure gain or pure phase variations, but not both simultaneously. Consequently, a system can display large, apparently safe gain and phase margins yet be vulnerable to instability from a small, combined gain-and-phase perturbation. A concrete example of such a scenario is detailed in [37]. This issue was less apparent when controllers were designed with graphical techniques, however, it has become a more pronounced concern with modern automated control design methods. Similarly, since a time delay added to a system can be modeled as a phase lag variable with the frequency, the DM fails to indicate potential low robustness against gain amplifications.

To overcome the limitations of classical GM and PM indicators, the disk margin is introduced to assess simultaneous gain and phase variations in a unified manner. This approach models uncertainty as a complex multiplicative perturbation and calculates the largest perturbation disk that preserves closed-loop stability. While a skew parameter can be used to adjust the relative weighting between gain and phase uncertainty, a symmetric disk (skew = 0) is frequently employed.

The application of disk margin analysis to MIMO systems, while theoretically feasible, presents practical efficiency challenges, particularly in real-time applications. Seiler et al. [37] discussed two methodologies: loop-at-a-time analysis, which evaluates isolated channels, and multi-loop analysis, which models simultaneous perturbations. The former can be an overly optimistic assessment of system robustness because it evaluates channels in isolation, so it may exhibit excellent single-loop margins yet be destabilized by small simultaneous perturbations in multiple channels. On the other hand, multi-loop disk margins effectively address simultaneous perturbations, however, their computation requires determining the smallest combination of independent gain and phase variations across all channels that can destabilize the closed loop. This involves solving an optimization problem at each frequency point in a dense sweep, a process that is iterative and computationally intensive, making it impractical for real-time applications.

A more unified assessment of a system’s tolerance to simultaneous gain and phase variations has been developed within the framework of H∞​ control theory. The normalized coprime factor (NCF) margin, also known in the literature as the generalized stability margin, quantifies the size of the smallest perturbation to both the plant and controller that will cause instability [38]. This metric offers a unified assessment of the system’s tolerance to simultaneous gain and phase variations into a single measure.

7-Conclusion

This work develops and demonstrates an online stability indicator based on the NCF stability margin that quantifies the robustness of the closed-loop system as the plant changes during testing and enables the adaptation of control techniques in response to those changes. While the indicator may be useful for detecting different types of adaptations, damage in the form of structural degradation is selected as a situation of interest to demonstrate its capabilities. For SISO settings, a closed-form stability boundary associated with specimen degradation is derived for the outer-controller loop and used to perform a sensitivity analysis, showing that more flexible structures are more susceptible to outer-loop instability caused by stiffness loss. A practical procedure is developed herein in which the indicator triggers a controller switch, and stability of the transition is ensured through the identification of a common Lyapunov function. An illustrative example based on a modified version of a benchmark problem confirms that the indicator provides an advance warning of diminishing robustness and potential instability, and that the controller transitions remain smooth, allowing the test to continue safely despite changes in the physical specimen. These results suggest that incorporating the proposed indicator into experimental systems can improve the tracking performance and expand the range of high quality real-time hybrid simulations, enable more complex tests that are prone to changes in the physical substructure, and improve both test reliability and equipment safety by reducing the likelihood of unexpected instability. Experimental validation of the proposed framework is currently in progress, and an expanded discussion of the associated practical issues and observations will be included in a future manuscript.
